div.p: Dear Shuckburgh: Secretary Dulles yesterday on his return from Paris filled me in on the discussions there and asked me to assume the responsibility here in the Department of reviewing the Israel-Arab relations problem, of formulating some ideas for bringing about a settlement, and of discussing with you the development of a common approach. Raymond Hare, until recently our Ambassador in Lebanon and a long-time expert in the area, presently Director General of our Foreign Service, has been asked by the Secretary to assist on this problem and at a later date may be able to devote more time to it. George Allen has just assumed his new responsibilities as Assistant Secretary for Near Eastern, South Asian and African Affairs and I will be going over the problem with him this coming week.

It is impossible to state now just how soon I will be in a position to meet with you. I would hope it might be sometime between the latter part of January and the middle of February. One factor that weighs heavily with us is that nothing be done which will endanger Eric Johnston’s visit to the area between January 23 and February 26 on the Jordan development project.

In any event I will be in communication with you early in January either through your Embassy here or through Walt Butterworth concerning the progress of our thinking here and a date for our discussions.
I have read with great interest your memorandum report to Sir Anthony on your impressions from your trip through the area. I was impressed by how effectively you went to the heart of the problem.

We share your strong desire to maintain absolute secrecy on this effort and have taken the most stringent measures to prevent leaks. It is already evident that it is too much to hope for 100% success. Just this morning the Minister of the Israel Embassy here went on a fishing expedition concerning general reports of UK-US diplomatic activities on this front. Walt Butterworth will undoubtedly have informed you of the contents of a telegram in which we informed him of the general response we are making to inquiries.
I am thoroughly aware of the well-nigh insuperable difficulties that lie ahead of us but it is obvious that the surest road to a defeat would be inaction.
I am looking forward to seeing you early in the New Year,

note.p: In telegram 3295 to London, Dec. 18, the Department of State informed the Embassy that, in response to inquiries about American and British diplomatic activities, the Department intended to reply that the United States had been and would continue to be in constant communication with other governments interested in promoting security and lessening tensions in the Middle East, and that, pending the achievement of a formal peace, the United States was constantly searching for arrangements that would help resolve specific problems and would contribute to the area’s economic development. (684A.86/12–1854)
